payload.text: A continued boom in late-stage and growth funding combined with a surge in seed-stage funding helped buoy venture investment in Latin America for the third quarter of 2026, Crunchbase data shows. All told, startups in Latin America raised a combined $1.3 billion across seed- and growth-stage deals in the three-month period ending Sept. 30. That was up 26% year over year but down 9% from the second quarter. For perspective, we charted out total investment, color-coded by stage, for the past 12 quarters below. Of the quarterly total, $757 million went into late-stage and growth deals, up 74% compared to the $435 million that flowed into such deals in the third quarter of 2025. However, that is down 21.3% from the $962 million in late-stage and growth rounds raised by LatAm startups in the second quarter. (Although it’s worth noting that Q2 2026 represented the most raised at that stage since the second quarter of 2022.) Mexico startups have raised $1.52 billion in venture funding during the first three quarters of 2026, per Crunchbase data. Notably, that’s about 40.7% more than the $1.08 billion Brazil’s startups raised in the same period. This is unusual as Brazil has historically been the largest recipient of venture funding in Latin America. Still, Brazil continues to attract a broad range of investors. “Over the past year, we have seen investments into Brazil from firms including Sequoia , Founders Fund , NEA , Battery and Tidemark ,” Allen Taylor , managing partner of Endeavor Catalyst , told Crunchbase News. “For several, this marked either their first investment in Latin America or their first in a long time.” Igor Piquet , Endeavor Catalyst’s vice president and head of Latin America, noted that Mexico drew more venture funding in the first half of 2026 than Brazil. But much of Mexico’s funding went to a few startups, he pointed out, while Brazil recorded many deals. “Investors are concentrating on a few Mexican winners, while Brazil retains the breadth,” Piquet said, adding that Brazil also leads in realized exits. Table of contents Outsized rounds An uptick in seed funding ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Methodology Glossary of funding terms Outsized rounds Several mega-raises took place in Latin America in the third quarter. And notably, the two largest funding deals were not for companies in Brazil or Mexico, which have historically raised the largest share of venture capital in the region. They also weren’t to fintech, which typically has the most funding recipients in the region, but rather to energy-related startups. Black Giant , the Chilean project company for EnergyX ’s Black Giant lithium project, raised $225 million in a July round at a reported $900 million valuation. And Colombia’s Erco Energía , a clean energy company that builds and operates solar power systems for homes and businesses, landed a $129 million Series C in August at a reported $600 million valuation. Mexico’s Kapital , an AI-powered financial services company, raised a $125 million Series C in September at a $1.6 billion valuation. Tru Arrow Partners led the financing, which included a senior debt funding facility provided by Fasanara Capital . And in August, Brazilian fintech Kesh Bank brought in $106.9 million in an equity and debt seed round at a $626 million valuation. Also in August, Brazil’s Decade , an AI-native wealth advisory company, landed $85 million in  what Crunchbase data shows is the largest seed funding deal ever raised for a Latin American startup. Founded by Vitor Olivier , former CTO of Nubank , and Felipe Meneses , founder of Hyperplane AI , the startup is backed by Benchmark , Greenoaks , Diffusion , Norte Ventures and Atlantico . An uptick in seed funding Latin America experienced a marked surge in very early-stage funding totals in the third quarter, largely thanks to the seed rounds mentioned above. Of the $1.3 billion raised by Latin America’s startups in the third quarter, about 20.5% — or $266 million — was raised across the angel and seed stages. That’s up 128% from the $117 million raised across those stages in the second quarter of 2026, and up 62% from the $165 million in the same quarter last year. Just over 22%, or $288 million, was raised at early stages, down 18.9% from $355 million in the second quarter and 34% from $437 million in the same period last year. We expect the Q3 deal counts to rise somewhat over time; however, as seed rounds in particular are commonly reported weeks or months after they close. ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Latin America is drawing renewed interest from international venture investors, according to Endeavor’s Taylor. He said international VCs were more active in the region, particularly Brazil, during the first three quarters of 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined, through both new investments and follow-on funding. “I joke that investors from the U.S. ‘rediscover’ Latin America every five or six years, and I think we are approaching another rediscovery moment,” Taylor told Crunchbase News. Endeavor Catalyst recently closed its oversubscribed $320 million fifth fund. Latin America accounts for nearly 40% of its portfolio by both deals and dollars, and Fund V had made 14 investments in the region as of Sept. 22. Taylor also pointed to opportunities beyond Brazil and Mexico, including repeat founders building global businesses from Colombia and emerging companies in Venezuela and Central America. Liquidity is improving, although acquisitions and secondary transactions are providing more opportunities than public listings, Piquet said. He pointed to approximately 60 private Latin American technology companies that have each raised at least $150 million as a potential pipeline for future IPOs. “The exit door is open, although it is not primarily opening through IPOs yet,” Piquet said. Taylor expects more exits could help bring global investors back consistently, with potential New York Stock Exchange listings by companies such as Wellhub , CloudWalk or Creditas contributing to another “rediscovery moment” in 2027. International investors remain interested in Latin America but have become more selective about deploying capital, according to Ana Cristina Gadala-Maria of QED Investors . Firms with a longstanding presence in the region remain engaged, while many that entered during the 2020–2021 investment boom have shifted toward AI opportunities elsewhere and are concentrating on existing portfolios, she noted. “Global investors are increasingly investing behind themes rather than geographies,” she said, putting Latin American startups in more direct competition with companies in the U.S. and other markets. Investor interest is increasingly centered on AI-native businesses and financial infrastructure, particularly stablecoins and cross-border payments. Gadala-Maria said more founders are targeting global markets from the outset, marking a departure from the previous wave of startups that adapted established business models to underserved local markets. “Increasingly, we’re seeing founders build globally competitive technology companies from Latin America, rather than necessarily for Latin America,” she said. Gadala-Maria agrees that Brazil and Mexico remain the region’s largest markets, with Brazil offering a deeper, more mature startup ecosystem and Mexico providing substantial room for financial services innovation. She pointed to Argentina as an overlooked market, citing its strong technical talent and founders building companies for global customers. Correction : Details regarding Kapital’s Series C were updated. The deal was a debt and equity raise. payload.text: By Anurag Gurtu Congratulations to the enterprise AI company that just raised another nine-figure round to solve a problem software is supposed to solve by itself: getting humans to use the product. You know the one. Won’t name it. Don’t have to. You’ve read the press release — “autonomous,” “agentic,” “category-defining” in paragraph one, and then, a few paragraphs down, where the money is actually going: hiring an army of engineers to sit inside customer offices and manually make the “autonomous” thing behave. Nothing says “we’ve built the future of work” quite like raising half a billion dollars to hire more people to do the work. The business model, decoded Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived. Here’s how it works, in case the deck was too artfully vague: Sell the customer an “AI platform.” Discover the platform doesn’t actually do the thing on its own. Send in the forward deployed engineers: sharp young people with CS degrees who now spend six months hand-building the workflow the website implied already existed. Bill the customer for “software.” Book it as ARR. Raise a bigger round because “ARR go up.” Repeat, forever, with an increasingly large and increasingly expensive engineering org standing between the product and the promise it made. This is not a flywheel. This is a payroll with a pitch deck. And the industry has stopped even pretending otherwise — it’s fundraising on it, loudly. OpenAI pledged up to $1.5 billion into a deployment joint venture valued at $10 billion, with another $4 billion from TPG , Bain Capital , Advent , Brookfield and Goanna . The vehicle, DeployCo, has been reported with more than $4 billion in investment. Meanwhile, job postings for “forward deployed engineer” are up somewhere between 800% and 1,000% year over year. Lightcast data reported by Fortune put the increase at more than 1,000% from January to August 2026. Financial Times data carried by PYMNTS put listings up more than 800% from January to September 2025, and Indeed data showed postings rising from 643 in April 2025 to 5,330 in April 2026. Total comp is pushing past $300,000 in the U.S. Employer postings list Anthropic at $280,000 to $320,000 base pay and OpenAI at $185,000 to $300,000 base, plus equity. Fortune reported some Anthropic roles reaching $400,000 in total compensation. Somewhere, a VC is calling this “operating leverage” with a completely straight face. It is not operating leverage. It’s a staffing agency that learned to say “agentic.” The tell Ask the one question the pitch deck conveniently never answers: “If you pulled the embedded engineer out tomorrow, does the customer still get what they paid for?” If the honest answer is “well, no, but the ARR is real” — that’s not product-market fit. That’s people-market fit, and people-market fit has a brutally unglamorous ceiling: You can only hire humans so fast, and you can never hire them cheap enough to earn a software multiple. Every new logo doesn’t get more profitable to serve. It gets another headcount request. Two companies, same $20 million ARR. One needs 10 engineers to keep the lights on. The other needs 100. Both slides say, “AI software company.” The difference shows up in gross margin, cost to onboard the next customer, and whether that cost falls as the company scales. The bill always comes due Here’s the thing about people-market fit: it feels great right up until someone asks the unfashionable questions: What does it actually cost, fully loaded, to onboard the next customer? Does that number go down as the company scales, or does it just grow the org chart? What happens to gross margin if the first year growth slows and the headcount can’t hide behind hypergrowth anymore? Companies funding their FDE armies with fresh nine-figure rounds are betting nobody asks these questions until after the round closes and the confetti is swept up. That’s a fine bet in a hype cycle. It’s a terrible one in a market that’s about to start reading the fine print. Because eventually, someone always reads the fine print. A CFO builds a cost-per-deployment model. A CIO benchmarks time-to-value against three vendors instead of trusting one demo. An investor finally does the unglamorous work of separating software ARR from human-powered ARR on the same balance sheet. The distinction buyers and investors can test is on the numbers. Software ARR should get cheaper to deliver as it scales. Human-powered ARR does not. OpenAI guaranteed the private-equity backers of its deployment vehicle an annual 17.5% return over five years, which is a different structure from a growth thesis.¹ So no, your AI isn’t autonomous. But your business model might be — autonomously transferring the cost of a services company onto a software valuation, for as long as the music plays. Enjoy the round. Hope the org chart was worth it. Anurag Gurtu , the co-founder and CEO of Airrived , is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk , Tripwire and Sun Microsystems , and a public company, FireEye . He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification. Illustration: Dom Guzman

Total funding is down substantially from the prior quarter, which was boosted by a $7.4 billion financing for China’s DeepSeek , but still the second-highest tally on record. For Q3, a couple of extra-large rounds bolstered the AI investment tally. The largest went to Beijing-based foundational model company Moonshot AI , which secured $3.5 billion in July at a reported $35 billion valuation. Kling AI , the AI spinout of China-based short video platform Kuaishou Technology , was the second-biggest fundraiser. The generative video startup raised around $3 billion in a July financing that included Baidu and Tencent . China leads by far in country-by-country breakdown China was the leading Asian destination for venture investment by a very wide margin. Per Crunchbase data, roughly $27 billion — or 70% of all Asian startup funding in Q3 — went to China-based companies. India was a distant second, with $2.9 billion, followed by Singapore, with $2.5 billion. For perspective, below we charted third-quarter startup funding tallies for the six countries with the largest totals. Late stage Most capital went to late- and growth-stage funding rounds. Per Crunchbase data, investment at this stage totaled around $20 billion in Q3. That’s down a bit from the prior quarter but nearly double year-ago levels and the second-strongest showing in four years. Multiple jumbo rounds kept the total high. The largest was Moonshot AI’s aforementioned $3.5 billion Series F. Several others raised financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. Shenzhen-based D-Robotics , a provider of robotics hardware and software, for instance, picked up $400 million in a September Series C. And Hong Kong-based Qupital , an e-commerce fintech platform, secured $300 million in Series C funding as it eyes an IPO. Early stage Early-stage investment drifted lower in Q3 but remained at historically high levels. Per Crunchbase data, financing for startups at the Series A and Series B stages totaled $13.6 billion for the just-ended quarter. That’s a decline of 28% from the prior quarter but up 65% from year-ago levels. Seed Reported seed funding hit its highest level in years, boosted by investor enthusiasm around AI. In total, investors poured $4.9 billion into reported seed and angel deals across Asia, per Crunchbase data. That’s up around 22% from the prior quarter and more than double year-ago levels. A big quarter for China Overall, Q3 was a robust period for venture funding to China-based companies, with far smaller sums going to other Asian startup hubs. Funding to startups based in India and Singapore was down significantly quarter over quarter, while Israel’s investment totals declined slightly. We’ll keep an eye out in the coming months to see if this divergence of fortunes persists. payload.text: By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. Illustration: Dom Guzman

Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter. Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider Keyfactor , which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners . Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage. Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners . The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion. Cyera , operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity -led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup. For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients. Exits, too We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish. Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age. Among private unicorns, meanwhile, Cyera proved it can find a way to spend a good chunk of the capital it raised. It acquired Oasis Security , an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion. As for public offerings, Aura , which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut. The Boston-based startup completed an acquisition of an Australian public company, Qoria , in July, and then renamed the combined company Aura. Overall, an upbeat quarter Overall, Crunchbase funding data points to an upbeat environment for cybersecurity startup funding. This doesn’t seem particularly surprising given the steady drumbeat of worrisome news about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI technology. It’s not an especially reassuring time for most of us. But for cybersecurity founders, there’s certainly an ever-expanding array of hazards to keep at bay. We’ll keep watching in the current quarter to see if investment momentum continues to build. payload.text: While helping another founder build an app that collected information about class-action settlements, Zim Hang came to learn how challenging it can be for consumers to seek compensation from companies they believe wronged them. He also discovered mass arbitration, a way to pursue individual claims when companies’ contracts prevent customers from joining class actions. At the same time, he also realized that relatively few law firms were set up to manage thousands of those claims at once. Zim Hang, founder and CEO of Chariot Claims. (Courtesy photo) That gap became the basis for Chariot Claims , which has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Silverton Partners to help consumers pursue claims over alleged privacy violations, hidden fees and subscriptions that are difficult to cancel. Indicator Ventures , Lightbank , Neon Fund , ZVC , Rosecliff Ventures , Alumni Ventures , FJ Labs , Graph Ventures and Vermilion Ventures also participated in the financing. The New York-based startup works with law firms to identify potential cases, find affected consumers and gather information needed to pursue compensation. The round brings its total funding to $15.7 million, which includes a $3.6 million seed investment in April 2025 and an earlier pre-seed round. Chariot’s latest round comes amid a surge in investment across legal tech. Funding to the legal tech space hit a record high last year, with $4.6 billion invested, per Crunchbase data . So far this year, legal tech startups have pulled in more than $3 billion, putting the sector on pace to match or exceed the 2025 total. The Chariot process works like this: For each case, consumers complete an intake questionnaire that assesses preliminary eligibility in real time. Chariot’s team then reviews these pre-qualified claims through a multi-layered system of technology and human oversight before sending it to the partner law firm handling the case. Hang, the company’s CEO, told Crunchbase News that Chariot typically receives more than 200,000 claim submissions per month and that it has taken on roughly 80 cases since shifting to its current business model just over a year ago. The company has about 15 employees and is currently breaking even, he said. It plans to spend the new funding primarily on hiring and product development, including AI tools to review cases and help determine whether consumers qualify to participate. A gap in consumer legal services Chariot is Hang’s third startup. His first company grew out of sleep research he conducted while studying psychology and neuroscience at Washington University . He turned that research into a smart-pillow business and later sold its intellectual property to a medical-device operator. He later worked in healthcare technology and fintech, founded a startup in the Web3 space, and then moved into legal technology. Across those industries, he said, he encountered complicated systems in which the interests of businesses and their customers did not always align. His experience helping the class-action settlement startup brought those concerns into focus. He described being “frustrated and mystified and horrified by how our justice system works.” Chariot started about three years ago, adopting its current model after Hang saw an opportunity to help law firms handle mass arbitration. Firms accustomed to class actions could struggle with the work required to manage large numbers of individual claimants, he said. “It’s just really inefficient for them to try to build workflows around 10,000 claimants or 100,000 claimants,” Hang said. Chariot handles parts of that administrative work, while its partner firms handle the legal claims. The startup charges the firms flat service fees, and they work on a contingency basis. Hang emphasizes that since it’s not a law firm, Chariot itself doesn’t file claims. It helps consumers pursue a variety of claims. Those claims include allegations that websites or apps tracked their information without consent, that companies added fees during checkout, or that businesses made subscriptions easy to start but difficult to cancel, for example. Finding evidence and drawing objections Chariot starts by looking for potential cases involving privacy violations, hidden fees and other consumer complaints. Its software scans public records, including federal court filings, and uses AI to analyze the allegations and prepare research for its partner law firms. That research includes legal memos based on publicly filed complaints. Chariot is also developing tools to track changes in laws and court decisions that could affect whether a case can proceed. The work remains in the early stages, with the goal of automating more of the research that associates and paralegals would otherwise do, according to Hang. Chariot reviews a few hundred potential cases each month, he said. It tests ads for about 30 potential cases to gauge whether it can find consumers who may have a claim, then selects roughly 10 to pursue more extensively with its partner law firms. Each case can involve many individual consumers, whom Chariot reaches through advertising and partnerships with consumer financial technology companies. To determine whether they have a claim, consumers must provide information to help assess it. For example, in the case of a data breach, that could be a notice from the company saying their information was exposed. For a hidden-fee complaint, it could include what they purchased, when they bought it, and how much they paid. Chariot is building AI tools to help review that supporting information and determine whether a consumer has a claim, according to Hang. The required evidence, and the difficulty of verifying it, varies by the type of alleged violation. The startup plans to make that step easier by allowing users to connect their email accounts so its software can look for relevant documents, rather than asking consumers to fill out forms.  Hang estimates that such improvements could help the company handle 10x to 100x its current claim volume. Companies push back Not everyone welcomes Chariot’s approach. Advertising for potential claimants has brought strong objections from some of the companies involved. In fact, Chariot has received cease-and-desist letters challenging, among other things, its use of company names and trademarks in ads, noted Hang. But he asserts that identifying those businesses is necessary to reach people who used their products or services. “As a part of our business, we need to mention the name of the company that has this alleged violation,” he said. Chariot reviews the letters with legal counsel and complies with demands it considers valid, Hang said. He declined to name specific companies for this article. His broader goal is to make alleged consumer abuses more costly for businesses. If more affected customers pursue compensation, he reasons, companies will have a stronger financial incentive to change those practices. “We want to make unethical unprofitable,” he said. Mike Dodd , general partner at Silverton, told Crunchbase News via email that his firm was attracted to Chariot’s vertical AI approach to working with law firms, which he called “exciting and defensible.” “It’s a greenfield market with space to expand horizontally and eventually into a generalized consumer legal AI solution,” he wrote. The firm was also drawn to what Dodd described as “a business model that aligns capitalistic incentives with access to justice.” “When a company breaks the law and breaks what it promises to its consumers, the consumer rarely seeks justice,” he added. “Chariot has built the technology to make individual consumer claims work at scale, and the team to operate it in a category where execution is genuinely hard.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Legal And Legal Tech Startup Funding In 2026 Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot , a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com , but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green , founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector . Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies. “It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added. The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw. Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch. “I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said. payload.text: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink , to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda , the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. title: Github
summary:
四台机器，一个页面，零次切窗。

我有四台机器在跑 ZCode：公司台式、家里笔记本、云主机、Mac mini。

以前最烦的不是看不到进度，而是看不过来。每台机器一个窗口，切来切去，上下文全断。想看眼 e2e、批个权限、补一句 prompt，得先把窗口找出来。

所以我写了个 Android 客户端。做完才发现，手机扫码只是入口，真正解决问题的是多机聚合：

手机扫码，一次绑定多台桌面；
手机本地起一个群控台 Web 服务；
同一 Wi-Fi 下，PC 浏览器打开这个地址；
每台机器一个独立会话，单屏 / 双列 / 四宫格随便切；
PC 直连官方云，不经过手机转发。页面不关，就能一直连着多台机器。
现在的日常：早上到公司，四台机器同屏。

左上：办公室 MacBook 在重构登录模块
右上：家里台式机在跑全量 e2e
左下：云主机在部署 staging
右下：Mac mini 在等我看 PR #42
不用 Cmd+Tab，也不用给每台机器开一个远程桌面。它不是远程桌面，只是把官方会话页聚合成一个多机控制台。

技术实现也很直接：WebView 承载官方手机页，扫码或通过深链接绑定，凭据只存本机，https + 官方域名白名单 + sid/hash 校验；群控台本质上就是把凭据下发给浏览器，让 PC 自己连官方云。

手机端本身也能单独扫码接管，通勤、出门、躺床上都能看进度、批权限、补 prompt。

适合同时开多台开发机、多环境跑 Agent 的人；只有一台机器的话，手机端扫码接管也够用。

非官方客户端，Android 8.0+，APK 5.7 MB，直接装。debug 签名，内测/自用没问题，别拿去上架。 代码在 GitHub / Gitee，欢迎 Issue / PR。

GitHub： https://github.com/woshihoujinxin/zcode-mobile-android 
Gitee： https://gitee.com/houjinxin/zcode-mobile-android

最近 GLM 降智严重，大家可以在本地配置好别的模型，推荐 DS

title: Github
summary:
项目地址： https://github.com/astralwaveorg/lyra
文档： https://github.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/tree/main/docs
镜像：ghcr.io/astralwaveorg/lyra:1.0.0

Lyra 是一个自托管的音乐库维护工具。它不下载音乐，也不接管播放，只维护你已有的本地文件。

**它主要做四件事**

- **歌词**：从 QQ 音乐、网易云音乐、LRCLIB 抓取，写入内嵌歌词和同名 `.lrc`；已有有效歌词默认跳过；支持逐行对比、批量采纳和撤销。
- **标签**：按 MusicBrainz 补齐缺失字段，逐字段显示本地值、来源值和冲突；冲突不会自动覆盖；缺 MBID 或候选有歧义时可以用 AcoustID 指纹兜底。
- **整理**：按 `艺人 / 专辑 / 音轨号 - 曲名` 生成路径；目录可多选，也可以多选排除；所有移动先预览，目标存在不覆盖，移动后为空的目录可以清理，支持批量撤销。
- **重复音频**：按“音频完全一致 / 同一录音 / 标题、艺人、时长相近”分类；只检测，不自动删除；删除进入回收站，可以撤销。

**为什么做这个**

我的曲库在 NAS 上攒了很多年，标签和歌词状态很乱。试过一些工具，最大的顾虑是一键写入之后不知道改了什么，冲突被直接覆盖，出错也退不回去。

所以 Lyra 的原则是：

- 写入前备份，只改目标字段，失败自动回滚；
- 所有移动先给出新旧路径，确认后才执行；
- 删除是移入回收站，不是直接抹掉；
- 重复音频只列出来，删不删由人决定。
- 当然尽可能自动处理，引入 AI 决策能力（我个人使用 MiniMax ）

**界面**（测试曲库）

![概览]( https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/main/docs/assets/screenshots/overview.png)

![重复音频分类]( https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/main/docs/assets/screenshots/dedupe.png)

`http://127.0.0.1:8080`。用户名 `admin`，首次启动的随机密码在 `data/initial-password.txt`，登录后先改密码。

**目前的限制**

- 版本是 v1.0.0 ，主要在我自己的曲库上验证，边界情况还需要更多样本。
- 支持 FLAC 、MP3 、OGG Vorbis 、Opus ； OGG / Opus 的封面写入还没做。
- QQ 音乐和网易云的可用性受地区、网络影响； MusicBrainz 公共 API 每秒最多一次请求，大库建议自建镜像。
- 单管理员，没有多用户权限（似乎也不需要）。
- 不会自动整理目录，也不会自动删除重复音频（手动处理，自动风险太高）。

**想听听大家的反馈**

- 部署有没有卡住或者什么问题
- 歌词或标签匹配有没有明显误判；
- 重复音频的分类是否合理，有没有把不该删的放进待删除；
- 移动端布局、文档和错误提示是否清楚。

回帖或提 Issue 都行。附上版本、部署方式和错误日志即可，记得去掉密码、Token 和私人路径。

payload.title: Lyra：自托管音乐库的歌词、标签与整理工具（开源程序，欢迎测试与 PR）
payload.content:
项目地址： https://github.com/astralwaveorg/lyra
文档： https://github.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/tree/main/docs
镜像：ghcr.io/astralwaveorg/lyra:1.0.0

Lyra 是一个自托管的音乐库维护工具。它不下载音乐，也不接管播放，只维护你已有的本地文件。

**它主要做四件事**

- **歌词**：从 QQ 音乐、网易云音乐、LRCLIB 抓取，写入内嵌歌词和同名 `.lrc`；已有有效歌词默认跳过；支持逐行对比、批量采纳和撤销。
- **标签**：按 MusicBrainz 补齐缺失字段，逐字段显示本地值、来源值和冲突；冲突不会自动覆盖；缺 MBID 或候选有歧义时可以用 AcoustID 指纹兜底。
- **整理**：按 `艺人 / 专辑 / 音轨号 - 曲名` 生成路径；目录可多选，也可以多选排除；所有移动先预览，目标存在不覆盖，移动后为空的目录可以清理，支持批量撤销。
- **重复音频**：按“音频完全一致 / 同一录音 / 标题、艺人、时长相近”分类；只检测，不自动删除；删除进入回收站，可以撤销。

**为什么做这个**

我的曲库在 NAS 上攒了很多年，标签和歌词状态很乱。试过一些工具，最大的顾虑是一键写入之后不知道改了什么，冲突被直接覆盖，出错也退不回去。

所以 Lyra 的原则是：

- 写入前备份，只改目标字段，失败自动回滚；
- 所有移动先给出新旧路径，确认后才执行；
- 删除是移入回收站，不是直接抹掉；
- 重复音频只列出来，删不删由人决定。
- 当然尽可能自动处理，引入 AI 决策能力（我个人使用 MiniMax ）

**界面**（测试曲库）

![概览]( https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/main/docs/assets/screenshots/overview.png)

![重复音频分类]( https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astralwaveorg/lyra/main/docs/assets/screenshots/dedupe.png)

`http://127.0.0.1:8080`。用户名 `admin`，首次启动的随机密码在 `data/initial-password.txt`，登录后先改密码。

**目前的限制**

- 版本是 v1.0.0 ，主要在我自己的曲库上验证，边界情况还需要更多样本。
- 支持 FLAC 、MP3 、OGG Vorbis 、Opus ； OGG / Opus 的封面写入还没做。
- QQ 音乐和网易云的可用性受地区、网络影响； MusicBrainz 公共 API 每秒最多一次请求，大库建议自建镜像。
- 单管理员，没有多用户权限（似乎也不需要）。
- 不会自动整理目录，也不会自动删除重复音频（手动处理，自动风险太高）。

**想听听大家的反馈**

- 部署有没有卡住或者什么问题
- 歌词或标签匹配有没有明显误判；
- 重复音频的分类是否合理，有没有把不该删的放进待删除；
- 移动端布局、文档和错误提示是否清楚。

回帖或提 Issue 都行。附上版本、部署方式和错误日志即可，记得去掉密码、Token 和私人路径。

项目刚发布，欢迎试用。

觉得有用的话点个 Star 就好。

title: Jev in action
summary: task classifier and auto model router in Keen Code

extra.author: mochow13
extra.original_title: Show HN: Jev in action – task classifier and auto model router in Keen Code

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

In Keen Code, a coding agent solo-developed by me, I have implemented a task-classifier using Jev and a simple auto-router based on the classification result. The article shares details about how it's implemented.

In short, it has a very simple idea:

- For every user message, ask Jev to classify the task in one of the three categories (simple, standard, complex) given current state of the conversation.

- Keen also asks Jev to put a probability on this question: "is this a new task?"

- Based on the result, Keen uses a heuristic to switch the current model to one of the three pre-configured models by user for the three categories

- To make the router work, users have to configure one model per task category inside the coding agent itself

The heuristic is also very simple:

When routing is enabled, Keen switches only if the selected-category probability is greater than 0.5 and either:

- new-task probability is at least 0.6; or - category probability is greater than 0.8 and the target category is a higher tier than the active routed model.

Thoughts and feedback are welcome. And if you are interested to know more about Keen Code, the repo can be found here: https://github.com/mochow13/keen-code

title: Maali
summary: Privacy-first personal finance app with a local AI analyst

extra.author: zukhan
extra.original_title: Show HN: Maali – Privacy-first personal finance app with a local AI analyst

story_text.value:
I never felt comfortable signing up for cloud budgeting apps and having them store all of my financial data on their servers. I also didn't find locally hosted options that I liked using.

That led me to build Maali (https://maali.app) over the past year. It is currently a Mac and Windows app that lets you track spending, budgets, recurring bills, income, net worth, and more. It stores all of your data on your computer.

You can bring your data in by either manually importing bank statement files (CSV/PDF), or by using SimpleFIN, a third-party bridge that you set up once and it keeps your data in sync. Since SimpleFIN introduces a third party that moves your data, I also added a power-user feature where Maali watches a folder (per account) and imports files dropped there, so you can automate downloads however you like and keep everything local.

It also has an optional AI analyst (local Gemma 4 E4B model) that provides commentary on your spending and flags anything unusual about your finances.

I realize that mobile is a big part of convenience for people. Maali lets you set up a phone web app over your own Tailscale network, paired by QR code. I'm also close to launching iOS/Android mobile apps that keep data in sync between the desktop/mobile apps using end-to-end encryption. My goal is to provide a great user experience with maximum convenience without sacrificing privacy.

The full app is free to use for 30 days (no card/signup needed). After that, if you find it useful and want to continue using it, it's $99 one-time. There's a live demo on the site (https://maali.app/today) with synthetic data so you can get a feel for it. Would love to hear any feedback that you have.

title: yarareads
summary: Open-source early-reading reader with phonics help

extra.author: zoozla
extra.original_title: Show HN: Open-source early-reading reader with phonics help

story_text.value:
My kid is 6 y/o and she is learning to read. She's moved through the basic phonics with Teach Your Monster to Read but was struggling with how repetitive it was. I wanted to give her some stories to read, but she still needed help sounding words out - and I wanted her to have the experience of sitting and reading by herself.

So I built this book reader app to allow her to click on the words, sound out the phonemes, and read by herself.

My 12 year old son wrote the first story, there's a cliffhanger at the end and he's working on the next section.

We're going to release more chapters and more stories in the near future.

And there's one other thing -

The reader has an MCP connection, so you can connect your Claude or ChatGPT or Grok, give them a PDF of a book you like (or even a set of scans done quickly with a phone camera) and have them import your favorite books into the app (private to your account, for your own kid, if you own the book of course).

The reader is free to use on its website and open source if you want to tinker and create your own version.

The included stories are under Creative Commons.

title: KiviDB
summary: a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache

extra.author: murtazayusuf
extra.original_title: Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache

story_text.value:
Hi all,

So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on.

Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out at : https://kividb.io, I open sourced the core engine under AGPLv3, didn't want to have just source available, because that is available with other tools too. It supports apprx 98-99% of the redis 8.10 commands, few have issues and you can find them at https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues, contributors are welcome.

Now the numbers, for the final benchmark, I used 2 c7gn.metal servers, in the same placement group in us-east1, and I used memtier-benchmark tool for this. The setting was : 10M keys, 100B each, 32 cores in use with both pipeline and un-pipelined runs.

pipeline 16 GET: KiviDB 21.2M ops/sec vs Dragonfly 2.0 9.1M, Redis 8.10 2.4M, Redis Cluster 32 shards 4.7M

When not pipelined, Dragonfly performed slightly better at 3.35M ops/sec vs kividb at 3.07M ops/sec. Memory per key was also slightly worse than dragonfly and almost same as Redis, 177B (kividb) vs 134B (dragonfly) vs 178B (redis).

With vector ingestion times it was slower but when querying, it was faster than most alternatives at lower ef, however slower than dragonfly at high ef. Most of the technical details are mentioned here so you can check it out: https://kividb.io/benchmarks.

easiest way to try it: docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb

I am looking forward to building a community around this, provide better rust based tools, I am open to constructive criticism and value informed opinion. Thanks

title: 3anddoneapp
summary: I built a task system to handle the drudgery so I could focus on tasks

extra.author: dmayle
extra.original_title: Show HN: I built a task system to handle the drudgery so I could focus on tasks

story_text.value:
I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done. It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do. It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long.

I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things. The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there).

When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others.

When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew.

That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work. Which was why I changed from system to system. Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day.

That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done.

This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said. My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building.

I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide. We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two). If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice. title: Pi-cowboy
summary: use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents

extra.author: suoloordi
extra.original_title: Show HN: Pi-cowboy – use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents

story_text.value:
pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi(https://pi.dev) and Herdr(https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead.

pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more.

Feature highlights:

- Foreign harnesses: pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest. Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system.

- Concurrency limits: You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control.

You can install it on Pi as a package:

  pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

extra.author: jsomau

story_text.value:
I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens.

Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild.

I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

title: Laminar (YC S24)
summary: RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces

extra.author: skull8888888
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar (https://laminar.sh). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark (https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling.

Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ

We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action

Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles.

Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough.

Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from.

Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things.

So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run.

flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full.

The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events.

Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them.

You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod.

Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar.

We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog (https://laminar.sh/blog) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction.

Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable (https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr). We make money from the managed cloud.

We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

title: Maxwell
summary: A new kind of model that sits between code and hardware

extra.author: laginimaineb
extra.original_title: Maxwell: A new kind of model that sits between code and hardware

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Gal from doubleAI. We've built Maxwell, a new kind of frontier model we call a Code Execution Model.

It sits between your code and the hardware. No humans in the loop! Maxwell makes the code run faster as it runs, without ever changing a single line.

Maxwell sees programs from the inside: traces, profiling information, and the data flowing through them. It adapts dynamically to the environment, including the hardware, what else is running, and what the inputs look like.

Code execution models change the way we approach coding. Today, Claude/Codex (and humans) keep re-optimising code for every different use-case hardware and data flow (think of LLM inference engines, like vLLM!). Our bet is that this is unnecessary, suboptimal, and that it does not scale. Instead, we think the right answer is to make code a living, thinking, thing.

Early access is open at heymaxwell.ai. Happy to answer questions here.

title: Ask HN
summary: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?

extra.author: rzk
extra.original_title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?

story_text.value:
I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...

> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too?

How are you handling this?

- Declare the input modalities of the VLMs that report text only (#49677) by @qgallouedec 
- Avoid a host-to-device copy in eager_mask (#49684) by @hmellor

summary: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available. Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. Practical applications With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model. What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic. Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints: Feature Purpose Use case JSON Schema

summary: Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments. This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click , which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
summary: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data. SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases: Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks. title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
summary: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
summary: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. title: AI 里没有答案的问题，需要一场「深谈」
summary: 去年，极客公园创新大会第一次办起「小场深谈」。场子都不大，百人左右围坐在一起。 有些瞬间仍然记忆犹新。 在「超级个体」专场，一位观众站起来。他刚从大厂跳槽到一家小厂，正用 AI 做自己的第一款产品。他向嘉宾说出自己的困惑：我还在打工，做公众号、视频号，早晚会被老板和同事刷到。这个冲突，怎么解？ 在「硬控 AI」专场，有人直接向刚刚离职的小米 AI 眼镜负责人提问：如果给你两个亿，你会去做哪种 AI 眼镜？有人继续追问，你觉得豆包手机助手到底是真需求还是伪需求？ 在「重塑关系」专场，一位精神科医生，问做陪伴机器人的嘉宾：你是希望它把人带回现实社会的交往，还是给这个家添一个新成员？ 这些问题都不「大」，但都很真，带着一个人具体的处境，来自坐在你旁边的人。 有老朋友说，这让他们想起极客公园 17 年前的样子——在借来的索尼探梦地下室里，一群人席地而坐。 如果你参加过去年的「小场深谈」，很可能还记得这种 Vibe。不是发布会式的提问，更像小场子里几个人围坐时，把一个人正在卡住、关心的事摊开来聊。 去年的「小场深谈」，共设置了 4 个主题专场，包涵 12 场深度访谈，数百位观众走进小场，165 个朋友甚至同时买了主舞台和「小场」的票：既听了主会场的趋势判断，也不舍得错过小场里「深谈」的收获。还有超过不少人专程为某一场深谈而来。 大会后的购票调研里，超过六成观众把「话题兴趣」排在首位，为了聊自己真正关心的问题而来。 这让我们确认： 在信息过载的时代，有些问题，听 AI 解释一百遍，不如和「最有料的人」当面聊一次。嘉宾谈得尽兴，观众提出高质量的问题，一场访谈变成真正的共同创作。 IF 2026「小场深谈」现场部分精彩瞬间 今年 12 月 5 日、6 日，极客公园创新大会 2027 将在北京举行，主题是「Revaluation 价值，另有答案」。 AI 冲击下，价值的标准正在被重新评估。哪些旧经验值得重新审视，哪些新机会正在出现？ 最迫切的那些议题，网络上、AI 里都没有现成答案。 因此，在主舞台之外，我们将继续保留「小场深谈」——一个更小、更近、更主动的交流空间： 更深： 围绕一个方向，几小时的深度访谈与探讨，把一个问题聊透； 更近： 实干派嘉宾与观众面对面，传递最坦诚的思考； 更主动： 你不只是听众，可以提问，成为这场讨论的共同创作者。 值得聊的话题也在跟着变。 目前，小场的具体主题与最终场次仍在筹备中，但一批 候选话题方向 已经摆上桌面。与其关起门来做决定，不如把选择权交给极客公园的朋友们： 具身智能： 机器人从演示走向落地，真正卡在哪里？让一线团队聊聊那些「只有做过才知道」的阻力与加速度。 硬件创新： AI 时代，一个好产品的定义和实现路径正在被如何重写？好硬件的「新图纸」和「新供应链」应该是怎样的？ Personal AI： 从「提醒你」到「替你办」。当 AI 开始持续替一个人做事，它能替你做到哪一步？我们又该如何与它相处？ AI 娱乐：
